extraction.name: FLORES-101
extraction.description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage) and professionally translated into 101 languages through a carefully controlled process with human quality assurance.
extraction.license: Sentences sourced from Wikimedia (Wikipedia, Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage) under permissive licensing

extraction.rai:dataCollection: Sentences were sourced from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage), manually selected by annotators, and then professionally translated into 101 languages by Language Service Providers (LSPs) through a multi-stage workflow including translation, automatic quality checks, and human quality assurance.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Sentences sourced from English Wikipedia, specifically from Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guide articles).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Sentence selection involved selecting articles at random, manually choosing 3-5 contiguous sentences per article, avoiding short or malformed sentences, balancing paragraph location (beginning, middle, end), and extracting metadata (URL, topic, boolean flags for hyperlinked entities and images). Sentences were manually labeled by sub-topic.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Translations were produced by professional Language Service Providers (LSPs). The workflow included: (1) translation by an LSP with internal editing, (2) automatic quality checks (language identification, copy detection, length check, fluency check, engine copy detection), (3) human quality assurance by an independent LSP using a Translation Quality Score (0-100 scale) based on error types (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, register) with severity levels (minor, major, critical). Translations scoring below 90% were sent back for re-translation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed using a Translation Quality Score (0-100 scale). Languages scoring below 90% were re-translated. 45 languages required re-translation, with an average of 1 re-translation and a maximum of 3. All 101 final languages met the 90% threshold. The largest error category was mistranslation.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators: 6 male and 4 female, with different roles (researchers including scientists and engineers, and program/project managers), originally from different regions: East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automatic checks included language identification, copy detection, length comparison, fluency check via language model, and detection of translations copied from commercial translation engines using sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU (spBLEU) similarity heuristics.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dev and devtest splits are publicly downloadable. The test set is available only through a publicly available evaluation server to prevent overfitting. The authors hope to continue expanding the number of languages covered.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to foster progress in machine translation for low-resource languages, which are spoken by the majority of the world's population. It enables evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation including regionally-relevant language pairs that are traditionally neglected.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: All source sentences are in English (translationese effects may exist for non-English source directions). Sentence selection was performed by annotators from specific demographic backgrounds. Topic distribution is skewed toward travel content (WikiVoyage). Some translators may have used commercial translation engines despite guidelines forbidding it, which was mitigated by automatic checks.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: All source sentences are from English Wikipedia, so non-English source translations are produced by human translators (translationese). Coverage is limited to 101 languages. Several languages considered for inclusion could not meet the 90% quality threshold. The dataset is intended for evaluation, not training.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use: evaluation benchmark for machine translation (many-to-many multilingual evaluation across 10,100 language pairs). Additional uses: document-level translation evaluation, multimodal translation evaluation, sentence and document classification, language identification, multilingual domain adaptation. The dev set is for hyperparameter tuning, devtest for development testing, and test set (via evaluation server) for final evaluation.

name.evidence: We present the FLORES-101 benchmark, consisting of 3001 sentences sampled from English Wikipedia and professionally translated in 101 languages.

description.evidence: We introduce the FLORES-101 evaluation benchmark, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and covering a variety of different topics and domains. These sentences have been translated in 101 languages by professional translators through a carefully controlled process.

creator.evidence: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzatoy, Francisco Guzmány, Angela Fanyz Facebook AI Research,zLORIA

inLanguage.evidence: We summarize all 101 languages in FLORES-101 and their scripts and language families in Table 4.

isLiveDataset.evidence: We hope to continue to expand the number of languages covered in FLORES-101 and make the test set available to various community efforts to improve translation systems in shared tasks such as those from the Workshop on Machine Translation.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: The construction of FLORES-101 is intended to accomplish several goals... the overall construction process consisted of three phases... First, we extracted sentences to translate from English Wikipedia. Second, we designed and ran pilot experiments to determine the translation process, and finally we launched the actual translation workflow for over 100 languages.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: All source sentences were extracted from multiple Wikimedia sources... The sentence selection process consisted of selecting an article at random from each source, and then manually selecting a few (typically between 3 and 5) contiguous sentences from each article... The selection process was performed by 10 different annotators in our lab.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: we collected a third of the sentences from Wikinews, which is a collection of international news articles, a third from Wikijunior, which is a collection of age-appropriate nonfiction books for children from birth to age 12, and a third from WikiVoyage which is a travel guide with a collection of articles about travel tips, food and destinations around the globe.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The sentence selection process consisted of selecting an article at random from each source, and then manually selecting a few (typically between 3 and 5) contiguous sentences from each article, avoiding segments with very short or malformed sentences. To avoid bias coming from the document structure, we carefully selected one paragraph per document, from either the beginning, middle or end of the article.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: We assess translation quality through a Translation Quality Score, calculated per language on a 0 to 100 scale... The following errors are examined: grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition or omission of information, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register. Each error is also associated with a severity level, between minor, major, and critical. Based on our pilot experiments, we set the acceptable translation quality score to 90%.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: All 101 languages in FLORES-101 meet our initial threshold of 90% quality based on human evaluation. Note that several languages were considered beyond our set of 101, but were unable to meet the bar after rounds of re-translation. Overall, about 50% of languages have fairly high quality (above 95%), with few near the 90% threshold boundary.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: The selection process was performed by 10 different annotators in our lab, 6 male and 4 female; with different roles in research: researchers (scientists and engineers) and program/project managers; originally coming from different regions of the world: East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America and North America.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: We implemented several checks to ensure the first round of translations were of acceptable quality: (i) language identification, (ii) checking whether the translation is a copy of the source sentence; (iii) checking whether the translation has significantly different length, (iv) checking translation fluency according to a language model, (v) and checking whether the translation is a copy of the translation produced by publicly available translation engines.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: The test set will not be released, but will be available via a publicly available evaluation server, while the dev and devtest are publicly downloadable. We hope to continue to expand the number of languages covered in FLORES-101 and make the test set available to various community efforts to improve translation systems in shared tasks.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Yet, the majority of the world's population speak low-resource languages and would benefit from improvements in translation quality on their native languages... This enables the evaluation of popular multilingual MT systems as well as the evaluation of regionally-relevant language pairs like Spanish-Aymara and Vietnamese-Thai.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: While translationese (or overly literal or awkward translations) has known idiosyncrasies (Zhang and Toral, 2019), we conjecture that these effects are rather marginal when evaluating models in low-resource languages... Among all checks, we found that (v) was the most significant issue, despite formulating clear guidelines forbidding the use of translation engines.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: By translating the same set of English sentences in more than hundred languages, we enable evaluation of multilingual MT with the only caveat that source sentences not in English are produced by human translators... Note that several languages were considered beyond our set of 101, but were unable to meet the bar after rounds of re-translation.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: FLORES-101 supports many-to-many evaluation, meaning any of 10,100 language directions can be evaluated. With rich metadata, it also supports multimodal translation via images, and document-level translation... Beyond translation, FLORES-101 can be used to evaluate tasks such as sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation.
